about: Celebrated space photographs, 1946 to 2022. `image` is tried first, then each `alt`, then the NASA Image and Video Library search `query`, then a styled placeholder. `verified` marks image URLs whose source page was confirmed when this file was written. Run scripts/fetch_gallery.py to mirror every image into site/assets/gallery/ for offline use.

items.title: The first photograph from space
items.mission: V-2 No. 13, White Sands Missile Range
items.credit: U.S. Army / White Sands Missile Range / Applied Physics Laboratory
items.story: A captured German V-2 launched from New Mexico carried a 35 mm movie camera to about 105 km (65 miles), shooting a frame every second and a half. The film survived the crash inside a steel cassette, giving humanity its first look at Earth from above the edge of space. Clyde Holliday, the engineer who designed the camera, said the pictures showed how the Earth would look to visitors from another planet.
items.query: V-2 rocket first photograph from space 1946

items.title: First look at the far side of the Moon
items.instrument: Yenisey-2 film camera with onboard development and scanning
items.story: Because the Moon is tidally locked, no human had ever seen its far side until Luna 3 swung behind it and photographed about 70 percent of it. The film was developed, fixed and dried inside the probe, then scanned and radioed to Earth. The grainy frames revealed a surprise: the far side has almost none of the dark lava plains (maria) that make the near side's familiar face.
items.query: Luna 3 far side of the Moon 1959

items.title: Ed White, first American spacewalk
items.instrument: Hand-held camera, photographed by James McDivitt
items.story: Ed White floated outside Gemini 4 for about 23 minutes, steering himself with a hand-held oxygen gun until it ran dry. He enjoyed it so much that mission control had to order him back inside, and he called going back in the saddest moment of his life. The photographs proved that astronauts could work outside a spacecraft, a skill Apollo would depend on.

items.title: Earthrise
items.instrument: Hasselblad 500 EL, 250 mm lens, Ektachrome film
items.story: On their fourth orbit of the Moon, Bill Anders saw Earth rise over the lunar horizon and grabbed a camera loaded with colour film. The picture of a small, blue, living world above a grey, dead one arrived as the environmental movement was taking shape. Nature photographer Galen Rowell called it the most influential environmental photograph ever taken.

items.title: Apollo 11 lifts off
items.story: The 110.6 m (363 ft) Saturn V left Launch Complex 39A with about 34.5 meganewtons (7.6 million pounds-force) of thrust from five F-1 engines. Roughly a million people watched from the roads and beaches around Cape Kennedy. Four days later two of its three passengers would walk on the Moon.

items.title: A man on the Moon
items.instrument: Hasselblad Electric Data Camera, 60 mm Zeiss Biogon lens
items.story: Neil Armstrong carried the main camera for most of the moonwalk, so nearly every famous Apollo 11 surface photograph shows Buzz Aldrin, not the first man on the Moon. Look closely at the gold visor: Armstrong, the lunar module and the photographer's own shadow are reflected in it. It became one of the most reproduced photographs of the twentieth century.

items.title: Bootprint in the regolith
items.story: Aldrin photographed his own bootprint as a soil-mechanics experiment: how deep a print sinks and how sharp its edges stay reveal how fine and compacted the lunar dust (regolith) is. With no wind or rain, prints like this can last for millions of years, slowly erased only by micrometeorites. A science record became a symbol of the whole programme.

items.title: The Blue Marble
items.story: Five hours after launch, from about 29,000 km (18,000 miles) away, the Apollo 17 crew photographed a fully lit Earth with the Sun behind them. Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and the Antarctic ice cap are all visible; the original frame actually had south at the top. It was the last time humans were far enough away to take such a picture until Artemis II in 2026.

items.title: A geologist on the Moon
items.story: Harrison Schmitt, the only professional geologist to walk on the Moon, stands beside a huge split boulder in the Taurus–Littrow valley during the third and final moonwalk. Apollo 17 brought back 110.5 kg (243.7 lb) of rock and soil, the largest haul of any mission. No one has stood on the Moon since.

items.title: First photograph from the surface of Mars
items.story: Minutes after touchdown in Chryse Planitia, Viking 1 scanned its own footpad and the rocks beside it, line by line. Engineers pointed the first picture at the ground so they could judge whether the lander was sinking into dust. It was the first photograph ever returned from the surface of Mars.
items.query: Viking 1 lander first image Mars surface footpad

items.title: Valles Marineris from orbit
items.instrument: Visual Imaging Subsystem, mosaic of 102 frames
items.story: The great scar across Mars is a canyon system about 4,000 km (2,500 miles) long and up to 7 km deep, long enough to span the continental United States. Mariner 9 discovered it in 1972 and it carries that mission's name. This mosaic was built from Viking orbiter frames by the United States Geological Survey (USGS).

items.title: Columbia's first launch
items.story: Exactly twenty years after Yuri Gagarin's flight, John Young and Robert Crippen rode the first Space Shuttle into orbit. It was the first time a crewed spacecraft flew with people aboard on its very first launch. On this flight and the next the external tank was painted white; later tanks were left rust-orange to save about 270 kg (600 lb).

items.title: The surface of Venus
items.instrument: Panoramic telephotometer camera with colour filters
items.credit: USSR Academy of Sciences / Lavochkin Association
items.story: Venera 13 descended through a crushing atmosphere, with a surface pressure about 90 times Earth's and temperatures hotter than 450 °C (840 °F), hot enough to melt lead. Designed to survive 32 minutes, it kept working for 127 and returned the first colour pictures from Venus. The orange tint comes from sunlight filtered through thick clouds of sulphuric acid.

items.title: Bruce McCandless, untethered
items.story: Wearing the nitrogen-jet Manned Maneuvering Unit (MMU), Bruce McCandless flew about 98 m (320 ft) away from Challenger with no safety line: the first untethered spacewalk. For those minutes he was, in effect, his own satellite. The image became a defining picture of the Shuttle era's ambition.
items.query: McCandless Manned Maneuvering Unit untethered EVA

items.title: Neptune and the Great Dark Spot
items.story: Taken days before Voyager 2's closest approach on 25 August 1989, this is still the best view humanity has of Neptune: no spacecraft has been back. It revealed the Great Dark Spot, a storm about the size of Earth, and winds of up to 2,100 km/h (1,300 mph), the fastest in the Solar System. Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune.

items.title: Pale Blue Dot
items.story: At Carl Sagan's urging, Voyager 1 turned around about 6 billion km (3.7 billion miles) from home and photographed Earth: a speck less than a pixel wide, caught in a scattered sunbeam. They were among the last pictures Voyager 1 ever took; its cameras were switched off soon after to save power. Sagan wrote that every human who ever lived did so 'on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.'

items.title: Pillars of Creation (Hubble, 1995)
items.credit: NASA, ESA, STScI, J. Hester and P. Scowen (Arizona State University)
items.story: Towers of cold gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula, about 6,500 light-years away, are being sculpted by ultraviolet light from nearby young stars; the left pillar is about four light-years tall. Released in November 1995, it proved that the repaired Hubble Space Telescope (HST) could deliver breathtaking science. The notched corner is the shape of the WFPC2 camera's four detectors.
items.query: Pillars of Creation Hubble 1995 Eagle Nebula

items.title: Hubble Deep Field
items.credit: R. Williams (STScI), the Hubble Deep Field Team and NASA
items.story: Director Robert Williams spent his own discretionary time pointing Hubble at an apparently empty patch of sky in Ursa Major for ten days. Colleagues worried nothing would show up; instead about 3,000 galaxies appeared, some seen as they were more than 12 billion years ago. It changed how astronomers study the early Universe.

items.title: The Sombrero Galaxy
items.instrument: Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS), six-frame mosaic
items.credit: NASA and The Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)
items.story: Messier 104 sits about 28 million light-years away and is roughly 50,000 light-years across, seen almost edge-on so its dust lane cuts across a brilliant central bulge. The bulge hides a supermassive black hole of about a billion solar masses. This mosaic became one of Hubble's most requested images.

items.title: Hubble Ultra Deep Field
items.instrument: Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) and NICMOS
items.credit: NASA, ESA, S. Beckwith (STScI) and the HUDF Team
items.story: About a million seconds of exposure on one tiny patch of sky in the constellation Fornax revealed roughly 10,000 galaxies. The faintest are seen as they were only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang. Extrapolated across the sky, fields like this imply the observable Universe holds hundreds of billions of galaxies or more.

items.title: The Helix Nebula
items.mission: Hubble Space Telescope and Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory
items.instrument: ACS plus the Mosaic camera on the Blanco 4 m telescope
items.credit: NASA, NOAO, ESA, the Hubble Helix Nebula Team, M. Meixner (STScI) and T.A. Rector (NRAO)
items.story: About 650 light-years away, a dying Sun-like star has shed its outer layers into a glowing shell, and the exposed hot core lights it up. Its resemblance to a giant iris earned it the nickname 'the Eye of God'. It is a preview of our own Sun's fate in roughly five billion years.

items.title: On the surface of Titan
items.credit: ESA / NASA / JPL / University of Arizona
items.story: The European Space Agency's (ESA) Huygens probe parachuted through Titan's orange haze and landed on Saturn's largest moon: the most distant landing ever made. The rounded 'pebbles' are chunks of water ice, smoothed like river stones, on ground dampened by liquid methane. It remains the only landing in the outer Solar System.

items.title: The Whirlpool Galaxy
items.credit: NASA, ESA, S. Beckwith (STScI) and The Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)
items.story: Messier 51 is a grand-design spiral about 30 million light-years away, tugging on a smaller companion galaxy at the end of one arm. The gravitational interaction compresses gas and triggers the pink star-forming regions that trace its spiral. In 1845 Lord Rosse sketched its spiral shape, one of the first galaxies recognised as a spiral.

items.title: The Crab Nebula
items.credit: NASA, ESA, J. Hester and A. Loll (Arizona State University)
items.story: Astronomers in China recorded a 'guest star' in 1054 that was bright enough to see in daylight for weeks. Its wreckage, about 6,500 light-years away, is still expanding and is powered by a pulsar: a city-sized neutron star spinning about 30 times per second. At release this was one of the largest images Hubble had ever made.

items.title: Hubble after its last service call
items.instrument: Hand-held camera from the Shuttle's cabin
items.story: Astronauts photographed the 13.2 m (43.5 ft) telescope drifting away after the fifth and final servicing mission, which installed new cameras, gyroscopes and batteries. Hubble launched in 1990 with a flawed mirror and was fixed in orbit in 1993, and the servicing missions kept it at the frontier of astronomy for decades. No human has touched it since.

items.title: Mystic Mountain
items.credit: NASA, ESA, M. Livio and the Hubble 20th Anniversary Team (STScI)
items.story: A pillar of gas and dust three light-years tall in the Carina Nebula, about 7,500 light-years away, is being eroded by the fierce light of nearby stars. Stars forming inside it fire jets of gas from its peaks. Hubble released it to mark twenty years in orbit.

items.title: The Sun in extreme ultraviolet
items.story: Since 2010 the Solar Dynamics Observatory has photographed the whole Sun every 12 seconds in several wavelengths of extreme-ultraviolet light, each tracing gas at a different temperature. False colour turns million-degree plasma loops over sunspots into visible arcs. The flood of data lets scientists watch flares erupt and forecast space weather.
items.query: Solar Dynamics Observatory Sun AIA extreme ultraviolet

items.title: Earth at night (Black Marble)
items.instrument: Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) day-night band
items.story: The VIIRS day-night band is sensitive enough to see a single ship's lights at sea. Stitched from cloud-free orbits in April and October 2012, the map shows where people live, the gas flares of oil fields and the dark gaps of deserts and rainforests. Scientists use such maps to track power outages, urban growth and fishing fleets.
items.query: Black Marble Earth at night VIIRS

items.title: The Horsehead in infrared
items.credit: NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)
items.story: In visible light the Horsehead in Orion, about 1,500 light-years away, is a dark silhouette. In infrared, Hubble looks through the dust and reveals the pillar's delicate, glowing edges. It shows how infrared astronomy unveils star birth that visible light hides, the principle behind the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

items.title: The Day the Earth Smiled
items.instrument: Imaging Science Subsystem (ISS) wide-angle camera, mosaic
items.story: With the Sun hidden behind Saturn, Cassini photographed the backlit rings and, 1.44 billion km (898 million miles) away, Earth as a tiny dot. For the first time people knew in advance their planet was being photographed from the outer Solar System, and thousands went outside to wave. The mosaic, released in November 2013, reveals faint rings rarely seen.
items.query: Day the Earth Smiled Cassini Saturn PIA17172

items.title: Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko
items.story: Rosetta became the first spacecraft to orbit a comet, reaching this 4 km 'rubber duck' in August 2014. Two months later its lander Philae made the first landing on a comet nucleus. Rosetta found that comet water differs from Earth's oceans, challenging the idea that comets delivered most of Earth's water.

items.title: Pillars of Creation (Hubble, 2014)
items.credit: NASA, ESA / Hubble and the Hubble Heritage Team
items.story: Nearly twenty years after the original, Hubble revisited the pillars with its sharper Wide Field Camera 3. Comparing the two images shows the structures changing, including a jet-like feature that moved over the intervening years. Released in January 2015, it opened Hubble's 25th-anniversary celebrations.

items.title: Andromeda, star by star
items.instrument: Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) and WFC3 mosaic
items.credit: NASA, ESA, J. Dalcanton, B.F. Williams and L.C. Johnson (University of Washington), the PHAT team and R. Gendler
items.story: The Panchromatic Hubble Andromeda Treasury (PHAT) resolved more than 100 million individual stars across part of our nearest large neighbour galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away, in a 1.5-billion-pixel mosaic. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid variable star in Andromeda and proved it was a separate galaxy far beyond the Milky Way. Andromeda and the Milky Way are expected to interact in several billion years.

items.title: Pluto's heart
items.instrument: Long Range Reconnaissance Imager (LORRI) and Ralph/MVIC
items.credit: NASA / Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory / Southwest Research Institute
items.story: After nine and a half years and almost 5 billion km, New Horizons flew 12,500 km (7,800 miles) above Pluto and turned a blurry dot into a world. The pale 'heart', Tombaugh Regio, includes Sputnik Planitia, a vast plain of slowly churning nitrogen ice. Pluto proved geologically alive, with mountains of water ice and a hazy blue atmosphere.

items.title: Blue sunset on Mars
items.credit: NASA / JPL-Caltech / MSSS / Texas A&M University
items.story: Earth's sunsets glow red because air molecules scatter blue light away. On Mars the reverse happens near the Sun: fine dust lets blue light through more efficiently in the forward direction, so the sky around the setting Sun turns blue. Curiosity watched it from Gale Crater.

items.title: Curiosity at 'Buckskin'
items.instrument: Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI) on the robotic arm
items.story: Rover 'selfies' are mosaics: the arm-mounted camera takes dozens of frames that are stitched so the arm itself mostly disappears. Engineers use them to check wheel wear and dust build-up, and scientists get the drill site in context. Curiosity has been exploring Gale Crater since August 2012.

items.title: Jupiter's south pole
items.story: Juno reached Jupiter on 4 July 2016 and entered a polar orbit that no earlier probe had flown. It found each pole crowded with clusters of cyclones, many wider than Earth, packed into geometric patterns. JunoCam's raw images are public, so many of the best Jupiter pictures are processed by citizen scientists.

items.title: The International Space Station
items.story: Leaving for home, the Soyuz MS-08 crew photographed the whole station, about 109 m (357 ft) end to end, the size of an American football field including the end zones. Continuously crewed since 2 November 2000, it is the largest structure humans have built in space. Fifteen nations take part through five space agencies.
items.query: International Space Station fly-around Soyuz MS-08

items.title: Asteroid Bennu
items.story: From 24 km (15 miles), OSIRIS-REx photographed Bennu, a 490 m rubble pile shaped like a spinning top. The surface turned out far rougher than expected, forcing the team to find a tiny safe patch to touch. In September 2023 a capsule delivered 121.6 g of its rock and dust to Utah.

items.title: First image of a black hole (M87*)
items.instrument: Eight radio observatories linked into an Earth-sized interferometer, 1.3 mm wavelength
items.story: Radio dishes from Hawaii to the South Pole observed in April 2017 as one virtual telescope the size of Earth. The glowing ring is gas swirling around the shadow of a black hole of 6.5 billion solar masses at the heart of galaxy Messier 87, 55 million light-years away. Its size matched Einstein's general relativity.
items.query: Event Horizon Telescope M87 black hole

items.title: Perseverance and Ingenuity
items.instrument: WATSON camera on the SHERLOC instrument (robotic arm), 62 frames
items.story: Perseverance photographed itself with the Ingenuity helicopter set down about 3.9 m (13 ft) away, days before the first flight. The rover is collecting sealed rock cores in Jezero Crater, a former lake bed, for possible future return to Earth. Its instruments are hunting for signs of ancient microbial life.

items.title: Ingenuity, the first Mars helicopter
items.story: On 19 April 2021 this 1.8 kg (4 lb) helicopter rose 3 m (10 ft) and hovered: the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. Its rotors spin about 2,400 rpm to bite into air about 1 percent as dense as Earth's. Planned for five flights, it made 72 before rotor damage ended the mission in January 2024.

items.title: Webb's First Deep Field (SMACS 0723)
items.story: Unveiled by US President Joe Biden, the first full-colour image from the James Webb Space Telescope covers a patch of sky the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length. The foreground galaxy cluster, seen as it was 4.6 billion years ago, acts as a gravitational lens, stretching distant galaxies into arcs. Hubble's deep fields needed days to weeks of exposure; Webb did this in half a day.

items.title: Cosmic Cliffs in Carina
items.story: The edge of the star-forming region NGC 3324, about 7,600 light-years away, looks like a moonlit mountain range; its tallest 'peaks' are about seven light-years high. Infrared light lets Webb see hundreds of previously hidden newborn stars inside the dust. The 'steam' rising from the cliffs is hot ionised gas blown off by intense ultraviolet radiation.

items.title: The Southern Ring Nebula
items.story: NGC 3132, about 2,500 light-years away, is a planetary nebula: shells of gas cast off by a dying star. Webb's mid-infrared view showed for the first time that the star responsible is hidden in dust beside a brighter companion. The shells record thousands of years of the star's final breaths.

items.title: Stephan's Quintet
items.story: Four of these five galaxies, about 290 million light-years away, are locked in a gravitational dance; the fifth is a foreground galaxy only about 40 million light-years from us. Built from nearly 1,000 separate image files, it was Webb's largest image at release. Webb traced shock waves and an active supermassive black hole in the group.

items.title: Our galaxy's black hole (Sgr A*)
items.instrument: Global very-long-baseline interferometry array, 1.3 mm wavelength
items.story: Sagittarius A* holds about 4 million solar masses and sits 27,000 light-years away at the centre of the Milky Way. Because gas whirls around it in minutes rather than days, imaging it was far harder than M87*, and required averaging thousands of reconstructions. It confirmed the object at our galaxy's centre is a black hole.
items.query: Event Horizon Telescope Sagittarius A black hole

items.title: DART's last look at Dimorphos
items.instrument: DRACO (Didymos Reconnaissance and Asteroid Camera for Optical navigation)
items.credit: NASA / Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory
items.story: Seconds before slamming into the 160 m moonlet Dimorphos at about 6.1 km/s (14,000 mph), DART sent back close-ups of its boulder-strewn surface. The impact shortened Dimorphos's orbit around its parent asteroid by about 33 minutes. It was humanity's first test of deflecting an asteroid.

items.title: Pillars of Creation (Webb, 2022)
items.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; J. DePasquale, A. Koekemoer, A. Pagan (STScI)
items.story: Webb's infrared eyes see through much of the dust that made the pillars look solid to Hubble, revealing thousands of stars. The wavy red lava-like edges mark newborn stars, only a few hundred thousand years old, firing jets into the gas. Three generations of telescopes have now photographed the same towers.

items.title: Orion, the Moon and a distant Earth
items.instrument: Camera on an Orion solar-array wing
items.story: On flight day 13, Orion reached 432,210 km (268,563 miles) from Earth, the farthest a spacecraft built to carry humans had ever flown. A camera on its solar array caught the capsule, the Moon and the small crescent of home in one frame. Artemis I's success cleared the way for the crewed Artemis II flight around the Moon in April 2026.
